# The Polymorphism Problem
<!-- Slide 4 -->

## Big Idea {.smaller}

- The computer should be able to choose which function to use with which class.
- We need everything covered so far to understand this.

::: notes
Slides 5–17

Thursday ended on a question: point a Person* at ava and call print(). Which version runs? Today answers it. Inheritance, overriding, pointers, and arrays of objects all come together here.
:::

## What's Going On Here?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}
~~~cpp
// inhComp.cpp -- inherit compposition?
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

class comp {
public:
    comp() { cout << "Comp class\n";}
};

class base {
public:
  comp test;
};

class child : base {

};

int main() {
  child s;
}
~~~
:::
:::

::: {.column width="40%" style="font-size: 60%;"}
. . .

~~~
Comp class
~~~
:::

::::

::: notes
A refresher on an inheritance hierarchy before today's material. Ask students to predict the output: main only builds a child, and child is empty.

Building a child builds its base part first (11.02); base has a comp member, so building base builds test, and comp's constructor prints. child has-a nothing of its own, yet it gets base's composed member through inheritance: composition and inheritance working together.

Bonus question: class child : base has no public, so child inherits privately (11.02's Forgot public). It still builds the same way; only access changes.

Full program: cpp/inhComp.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 6 -->

---



:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="62%"}
::: {style="font-size: 45%;"}
~~~cpp
enum class Discipline { ARCHEOLOGY, BIOLOGY, COMPUTER_SCIENCE, };

class Person {
protected:
    string name;
public:
    Person() { setName("");}
    Person(const string& pName) {setName(pName);}
    void setName(const string& pName) {name = pName;}
    string getName() const {return name; }
};

class Student : public Person{ ... };

class Faculty : public Person{
  private:
    Discipline department;
  public:
    void setDepartment(Discipline d) {department = d; }
    Discipline getDepartment() const {return department; }
};

int main(){
    // Setup arrays to print enumerations
    const string dName[] = {"Archelogy", "Biology", "Computer Science"};

    Faculty* prof = new Faculty();                   // instantiate faculty
    prof->setName("Indiana Jones");                  // Msg to set name
    prof->setDepartment(Discipline::ARCHEOLOGY);     // Msg to set department

    cout << "Professor " << prof->getName()
        << " teaches in the " << "Department of ";

    Discipline dept = prof->getDepartment();             // Msg to get department
    cout << dName[static_cast<int>(dept)] << endl;       // Print Dpt in string form

    delete prof;                                     // we called new, so we delete
    return 0;
}
~~~
:::
:::

::: {.column width="38%" style="font-size: 60%;"}
. . .

~~~
Professor Indiana Jones
teaches in the Department
of Archelogy
~~~

- Recall: this worked because we set up a pointer of the proper type.
:::

::::

::: notes
Review of the Person hierarchy from inheritance week. prof is a Faculty*, pointing at a Faculty, so every -> call finds the function it expects. setName() and getName() come from Person; setDepartment() and getDepartment() from Faculty. The enum class Discipline is printed through the dName array, indexed by static_cast<int>.

This version uses a raw pointer, so it must delete prof; the original used shared_ptr, which deletes for you. Keep "a pointer of the proper type" in mind: Topic 3 points a parent pointer at child objects.

Full program: cpp/faculty_pointer.cpp
:::

## Arrays of Class Objects

::: {style="font-size: 50%;"}
~~~cpp
class Faculty : public Person{
  private:
    Discipline department;
  public:
    Faculty();    // total waste
    Faculty(const string& fname, Discipline d) : Person(fname){
        department = d;
    }
    void setDepartment(Discipline d) {department = d; }
    Discipline getDepartment() const {return department; }
};

int main(){
  Faculty arrFac[] = {Faculty("Bob Smith", Discipline::BIOLOGY),
                      Faculty("Indiana Jones", Discipline::ARCHEOLOGY),
                      Faculty("Ida Lovelace", Discipline::COMPUTER_SCIENCE),
                      };
  PrintLine(arrFac[0]);
  PrintLine(arrFac[1]);
  PrintLine(arrFac[2]);
  return 0;
}

void PrintLine(const Faculty& fac) {
  // Setup arrays to print enumerations
  const string dName[] = {"Archelogy", "Biology", "Computer Science"};
  cout << "Professor " << fac.getName()
      << " teaches in the " << "Department of ";
  cout << dName[static_cast<int>(fac.getDepartment())] << endl;
}
~~~
:::

- Still worked because all the objects are in the same class.

::: notes
Next: an array of Faculty objects is not much of a leap. Other languages do this. Person and Student are in the full program.

Output:
Professor Bob Smith teaches in the Department of Biology
Professor Indiana Jones teaches in the Department of Archelogy
Professor Ida Lovelace teaches in the Department of Computer Science

Full program: cpp/faculty_array.cpp (11-22m2.cpp)
:::

## Add a Student to the Array

~~~cpp
Faculty arrFac[] = {Faculty("Bob Smith", Discipline::BIOLOGY),
                    Faculty("Indiana Jones", Discipline::ARCHEOLOGY),
                    Faculty("Ida Lovelace", Discipline::COMPUTER_SCIENCE),
                    Student("Sam", Discipline::BIOLOGY, nullptr)
                    };
~~~

- g++: `conversion from 'Student' to non-scalar type 'Faculty' requested`
- Didn't compile because the array is not the same type as the Student object.

::: notes
Then we got the bright idea to add students to our array. Now we have two different kinds of objects, but they are related by inheritance: both are Persons. We have an inheritance hierarchy going on. Can we use that?

Full program: cpp/faculty_student_array.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 9 -->

---

## Point

- You can have arrays and vectors of class objects.
- However, you cannot take advantage of the inheritance hierarchy if you do so.

> Polymorphic code produces different behavior from different data.
>
> — Textbook, p. 955

::: notes
This is the rest of the lecture in one line: one piece of code, a loop over an array, that does the right thing for each kind of object in it.
:::

<!-- Slide 10 -->

---

## The Problem

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}
- We want to be able to call ANY of these objects AND have them execute behavior specific to that object.
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
![](images/person_hierarchy.png){style="max-height: 50vh;" fig-alt="Inheritance hierarchy: Person at the top, with Faculty and Student below it, and TFaculty below Faculty."}
:::

::::

::: notes
TFaculty is faculty with a title, such as Dr. or Professor. Topic 4 comes back to this hierarchy with inheritance4.h and inheritance5.h.
:::

<!-- Slide 11 -->

---

## How?

- Each class can be assigned to arrays of its own type.
- The Child Class can always be **assigned** to the Parent class.
- The Parent Class can be **cast** to the Child Class.
- **Polymorphism** can be used for all members of the inheritance hierarchy.

::: notes
This is type compatibility in an inheritance hierarchy, textbook section 15.1. A Student is a Person, so a Student can be assigned to a Person. Watch what that assignment keeps: only the Person part. Topic 2 shows why that matters.

Casting a Parent to a Child compiles with static_cast, but it is only safe when the object really is that child. 14.01 covers dynamic_cast, which checks.
:::

<!-- Slide 12 -->

## Security Hierarchy

![](images/security_hierarchy.png){style="max-height: 60vh;" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Inheritance hierarchy: HASH at the top, with TOY and SHA-256 below it, and SHA-3 below SHA-256."}

::: notes
A second hierarchy, with less baggage than Person. Every hash takes plain text and displays a hash of it; each kind of hash does that differently. The SHA classes print a placeholder instead of a real hash.
:::

<!-- Slide 13 -->

---

## The Security Hierarchy in Code

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="62%"}
::: {style="font-size: 50%;"}
~~~cpp
class Hash {
protected:
  string plainText;
public:
  Hash(string str = "Empty") {plainText = str;
      cout << endl;  // prints a blank line each time a Hash is built
                     }
  void Display(){cout << "Base text: " << plainText << endl;};
};

class Toy : public Hash {
public:
    Toy(const string& s) : Hash(s){};
  void Display() {
    unsigned int hash = 0;
    for (char c : plainText)
      hash = hash * 31 + c;  // Simple multiplicative hash algorithm
    cout << "Toy Hash of '" << plainText << "': " << hash << endl;
  }
};

class SHA256 : public Hash { ... };

class SHA3 : public SHA256 { ... };

int main() {
  Hash h("Welcome");
  h.Display();

  Toy t("Complex text");
  t.Display();

  SHA256 sha("More text");
  sha.Display();

  SHA3 sha3("Almost done");
  sha3.Display();

return 0;
}
~~~
:::
:::

::: {.column width="38%" style="font-size: 50%;"}
. . .

~~~
Base text: Welcome

Toy Hash of 'Complex text': 4101018301

SHA-256 Hash of 'More text': ***SHA-256***

SHA-3 Hash of 'Almost done': ***SHA-3***
~~~
:::

::::

::: notes
Each child overrides Display(), as in 12.01. Called on its own object, each one runs its own version.

The blank lines come from the cout << endl in Hash's constructor, which runs every time any of these objects is built.

SHA256 and SHA3 each have a constructor that passes the text up and a Display() that prints a placeholder; see the full code.

Full code: cpp/hash_classes.h and cpp/hash_demo.cpp
:::

## Now, Put It into an Array

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {style="font-size: 55%;"}
~~~cpp
int main() {
  Toy myToys[3]{Toy("Hello World"), Toy("Semper Fi"),
    Toy("The happiness of your life depends upon the quality of your thoughts.")};

  for (auto h : myToys) h.Display();

return 0;
}
~~~
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%" style="font-size: 50%;"}
. . .

~~~
Toy Hash of 'Hello World': 3432422020
Toy Hash of 'Semper Fi': 1492142785
Toy Hash of 'The happiness of your life
depends upon the quality of your
thoughts.': 2918282123
~~~
:::

::::

::: notes
An array of Toys, displayed by Toy's Display(). Every object is the same class, so this works, just like the Faculty array.

The output also starts with blank lines from Hash's constructor.

Full program: cpp/hash_toy_array.cpp
:::

## Now, Put It into an Array of the Parent Class

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {style="font-size: 55%;"}
~~~cpp
int main() {
  Hash myToys[3]{Toy("Hello World"), Toy("Semper Fi"),
    Toy("The happiness of your life depends upon the quality of your thoughts.")};

  for (auto h : myToys) h.Display();

return 0;
}
~~~
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%" style="font-size: 50%;"}
. . .

~~~
Base text: Hello World
Base text: Semper Fi
Base text: The happiness of your life
depends upon the quality of your
thoughts.
~~~
:::

::::

::: notes
Ask students to predict before revealing. The only change is Toy myToys[3] to Hash myToys[3]. It compiles, because a child can always be assigned to its parent, but every object now runs Hash's Display(). The Toys are no longer Toys.

Full program: cpp/hash_parent_array.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 16 -->

---

## Summary

- An array of one class works; a child can be assigned into an array of its parent, but then each element behaves like the parent.
- Polymorphic code should produce different behavior from different data, and so far it does not.

::: notes

:::
